name: Adam Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Harbour Street Garage, which is a normal six-bay place that went heavy on electric cars about three years ago. I'm the battery and electrics guy. Most mornings I'm testing cells on a battery pack or chasing a charging fault, and afternoons it's whatever's on the board, brakes, tyres, a service. I use an AI assistant all day, honestly, for wiring diagrams, fault trees and even writing up the job notes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, 27, I share a house with my mate Theo who's a sound engineer. I've got a decent amount saved, plus a share in a little allotment co-op, of all things. I read a lot about worker co-ops and I'd love to run a garage that way one day, where the mechanics own the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Then I'd have been very excited about nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a great tool, just not a revolution. I'd probably post a thread about how the useful bits got buried under the hype. At work I'd keep showing the others the tricks I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, if I'm honest. I like new stuff. But my job would be totally safe, and the electric car side of the trade keeps growing whatever AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using the assistant for diagrams and notes. Put money into the co-op garage idea, maybe start talking seriously with two of the lads about it. Do the advanced battery course in the spring, about 1,800, which I'd pay myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit bored. Then I'd find something else to be excited about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay for the course yourself. Why not ask the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because then it's mine. If I'm going to start my own place one day, I want the papers in my name and no strings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How serious is the co-op idea, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Serious enough that I've got a spreadsheet. Three mechanics, a rented unit on the trading estate and 30,000 between us would get a co-op garage open. I'm about a third of the way there on my own.

say: I'd call AI a **great tool**, just not a revolution.
I'd post that the **useful bits** got buried under the hype.
think: I'd be a little **disappointed**, because I enjoy new technology.
My job stays safe, and **electric car** work keeps growing anyway.
do: Keep using the **AI assistant** for diagrams and job notes.
Pay **1,800** myself for the advanced battery course in spring.
Start serious talks about a **co-op garage** with two colleagues.
feel: **Calm** and a bit bored, ready to find the next interest.
S0.quote: Three mechanics, a rented unit on the trading estate and 30,000 between us would get a co-op garage open.
fieldNote: He funds his own training to keep **independence** for a future business.
The **co-op garage** plan is concrete, with a spreadsheet and a target.
His disappointment shows he **welcomes change** rather than fears it.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant for wiring diagrams and notes
Pay 1,800 for the advanced battery course in spring
Save towards a 30,000 co-op garage with two colleagues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd actually bet on. I can already see half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure workers own the tools, not just rent them from the bosses. Online I'd be the annoying one posting about co-ops and unions in the same breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm on the right side of it. I already use the tools, I do the electric work, and the hands-on half of my job lasts a long while yet. I'd worry more about the parts and booking side of the garage than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in. Get the garage to use AI for quotes and parts properly, and show the lads how. I'd push the co-op plan forward a year, because a small garage that uses these tools well could undercut the chains. And I'd join the union, partly to argue that the time saved should go to workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly excited. A bit guilty about the people it'll hit harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would it hit harder, at Harbour Street?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo on bookings and parts. Our booker Jo is brilliant with customers, but her whole job is phone calls and parts orders, and a chatbot already does both. I'd want her in the co-op, doing something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd show the lads. Would they listen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. Big Sam would tell me to get lost. That's fine, I'd just show him how it found a fault in ten minutes that took him an afternoon.

say: I'd say workers must **own the tools**, not just rent them from bosses.
Online I'd post about **co-ops** and unions in the same breath.
think: I'm on the **right side** of this, already using the tools daily.
The **booking and parts** side of the garage is more exposed than me.
do: Set up AI for **quotes and parts** at the garage and train colleagues.
Bring the **co-op plan** forward by a year.
Join the **union** to argue saved time should go to workers.
feel: **Calm** and excited, with some guilt about colleagues hit harder.
S1.quote: Our booker Jo is brilliant with customers, but her whole job is phone calls and parts orders, and a chatbot already does both.
fieldNote: He wants to **bring AI in** himself, but on workers' terms.
He spots the **booker's** job as most exposed and wants to include her.
His calm comes from **skills and savings**, not denial.

steps.text: Set up AI quoting and parts ordering at Harbour Street
Bring the co-op garage launch forward by a year
Join the union and argue saved hours should go to staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That changes things. Two years is fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need a universal basic income, or something like it, and fast. I'd go on marches. I'd also say the gains should be shared, through public ownership if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking side of my job, the diagnosis and the electrics puzzles, goes in 2028. I'd still have my hands until about 2031. So I'd have three years of being a very good pair of hands, and then the robots come for those too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the co-op garage plan, because a new garage needs ten years to pay off, not three. I'd keep the savings in cash. I'd try to get into robot repair and setup straight away, because that's the next puzzle. And I'd join every campaign for a basic income I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited by the technology and scared about the money, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a big plan to drop. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutting. I spent two years planning a co-op garage, and I'd be shredding the spreadsheet because the robots would beat it to the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robot repair. How long does that last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe five years, maybe until the robots fix each other. I'm under no illusions. But I'm 27, I'd rather ride it than stand still.

say: I'd call for a **basic income**, and fast.
I'd march for gains to be **shared**, through public ownership if needed.
think: My **diagnosis** skills go in 2028, and my hands around 2031.
That leaves **three years** as a good pair of hands before robots arrive.
do: Drop the **co-op garage** and keep savings in cash.
Move into **robot repair** and setup straight away.
Join every **basic income** campaign I can find.
feel: **Anxious**, excited by the technology and scared about the money at once.
S2.quote: I spent two years planning a co-op garage, and I'd be shredding the spreadsheet because the robots would beat it to the door.
fieldNote: Even an **early adopter** loses his business plan in this picture.
He sees robot repair as a **short bridge**, not a safe harbour.
Politically he moves from **co-ops** to basic income.

steps.text: Shelve the co-op garage and keep savings in cash
Train in robot setup and repair this year
Join basic income campaigns and go on the marches

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a different game. I can work with five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set up shared ownership before it's too late. Co-ops, unions, a public stake in the big AI firms, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the garage could still work if it owns its own robots. The thinking part goes in 2031, the hands-on part around 2034. A co-op that buys a robot early and keeps the mechanics as owners could actually do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the co-op in 2027, small, with two others. Put AI in from day one for quotes and diagnosis. Save hard so we can buy robots as soon as they're good enough, and train ourselves to run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. This is the version where people like me get a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to customers when everyone's income is shaky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that worries me. People still need cars fixed, but they'll put it off. A co-op garage only survives if people can still afford to fix their cars, and that depends on wages I can't control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Theo be part of your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh and say sound engineers are next. He's probably right. We'd talk about pooling money, maybe buying the house we rent.

say: I'd say there are **five years** to set up shared ownership.
I'd back co-ops, unions and a **public stake** in AI firms.
think: A co-op that **owns its robots** could do well after 2034.
The **thinking part** of the job goes in 2031, but owners can keep income.
do: Open a small **co-op garage** in 2027 with two partners.
Put **AI** in from day one for quotes and diagnosis.
Save to **buy robots** early and train to run them.
feel: **Uneasy**, but more excited than scared about his chance.
S3.quote: A co-op garage only survives if people can still afford to fix their cars, and that depends on wages I can't control.
fieldNote: Five years turns the co-op from **dream to plan**.
His real worry is **customer wages**, not the machines.
He would **automate** his own co-op to keep owners earning.

steps.text: Open a small co-op garage in 2027 with two partners
Use AI for quotes and diagnosis from the first day
Save a robot fund for the co-op from monthly profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's the one where you can actually build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse to leave workers behind with ten years' warning. I'd campaign for every garage to have worker shares in any robots they buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine for the first eight years or so. I'd be 37 when AGI lands and 40 when the robots do. By then I'd want to own a slice of the place I work, not be paid by the hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same co-op plan, but grow it slowly, maybe a second site by 2032. Keep learning every new tool. Put part of my savings into the co-op and part into a pension, so I'm not betting everything on one garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a mild way. More like a big project with a deadline than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not betting everything. What's the hedge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pension and maybe a share in the house. I believe in the co-op garage, but I'm not daft enough to put my whole life in one rented unit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell an apprentice starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the electrics and learn the AI, and learn how a business works. The ones who only know the spanner will have the hardest time.

say: I'd say ten years' warning leaves **no excuse** to abandon workers.
I'd campaign for **worker shares** in any robots garages buy.
think: I'd feel fine for about **eight years** before the change lands.
By 40 I'd want to **own a slice** of my workplace, not be paid hourly.
do: Grow the co-op slowly, with a **second site** by 2032.
Split savings between the co-op and a **pension**.
Keep learning **every new tool** as it appears.
feel: **Uneasy** in a mild way, like a big project with a deadline.
S4.quote: I believe in the co-op garage, but I'm not daft enough to put my whole life in one rented unit.
fieldNote: He **hedges** the co-op with a pension, showing caution under the enthusiasm.
His advice to apprentices stresses **business skills** as well as tools.
Ownership, not wages, is his **answer** to automation.

steps.text: Open a second co-op garage site by 2032
Pay into a pension alongside the co-op stake

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it kills the co-op before it starts. What would help is cheap loans for workers to buy into their own garages, and some kind of basic income underneath. I'm not scared of robots in the workshop, I'm scared of robots that only the big chains can afford.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether customers will trust a robot with their brakes. I think a lot of them won't, at first. That might buy us more time than the dates suggest.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of robots in the workshop, I'm scared of robots that only the big chains can afford.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old** battery and electrics specialist who uses AI tools all day.
He is single, has **solid savings** and dreams of a worker-owned co-op garage.
He wants workers to **own the tools**, and backs unions, co-ops and basic income.
He stays **calm** in the milder pictures and grows anxious only when AGI comes in two years.
With more time, he plans to **automate** his own co-op so the mechanics share the gains.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would kill his co-op garage before it starts.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **loans** for workers to buy into garages, with a **basic income** underneath.
